meta.date: ~600 BC (before the departure from the valley)

world_behind.title: A family they already knew
world_behind.text: The sons go straight to "the house of Ishmael" (v. 4), gain a hearing, and persuade an entire household to abandon Jerusalem, a result that makes best sense if the families were already connected, perhaps by long acquaintance or existing marriage expectations. The record spends one verse on what must have been an extraordinary negotiation.

world_behind.title: Jeremiah in prison dates the chapter
world_behind.text: Nephi's evidence that the city's probation is closing is current news: "Jeremiah have they cast into prison" (v. 14). Jeremiah's imprisonments under Zedekiah are documented in his own book (Jer. 37–38), and the detail pins the record's chronology to checkable public history.

cites.quote: Jeremiah have they cast into prison

spans.text: Jeremiah have they cast into prison

world_behind.title: What the rebels were giving up, again
world_behind.text: For Ishmael's older children the journey meant walking away from property, betrothal prospects, and standing — the same ledger Laman kept in chapter 2. The desire to "return unto the land of Jerusalem" (v. 7) was not perversity; it was the era's ordinary arithmetic, aimed at a city with a decade to live.

cites.quote: return unto the land of Jerusalem

spans.text: return unto the land of Jerusalem

world_behind.title: Abandonment as execution
world_behind.text: Binding a man and leaving him "to be devoured by wild beasts" (v. 16) was murder with no blood on anyone's hands and no body to answer for. The plan's cold practicality, an untraceable death in empty country, is part of the record's honesty about how far the family's division had gone.

world_behind.title: Five daughters, three sons, and a colony's future
world_behind.text: The Lord's instruction that the sons "should take daughters to wife, that they might raise up seed unto the Lord" (v. 1) frames marriage as covenant demography: a promised land is no inheritance without heirs. Jeremiah wrote the same instruction to the exiles in Babylon that same generation — take wives, bear children, be increased (Jer. 29:6).

world_behind.title: The flood formula
world_behind.text: "the Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them" (v. 14) quotes the sentence spoken over the generation of Noah (Gen. 6:3). Hearers raised on the brass plates would catch the echo: Jerusalem is being cast as the doomed world, and the family as the remnant already aboard.

cites.quote: the Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them

spans.text: the Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them

words.text: "it was not meet for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone" (v. 1) means fit, suitable, proper. The word carries heaven's assessment of a solitary colonization: not wrong but unfit, a plan that cannot carry the promise it exists for. The correction is practical before it is doctrinal, and the errand it launches supplies the colony's future.

cites.quote: it was not meet for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone

spans.text: it was not meet for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone

words.text: "we did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael" (v. 4): a diplomacy word. After chapters of lots, gold, and a sword, the second Jerusalem errand runs entirely on goodwill and softened hearts. The contrast is the point: what the record's God does to Laban and what he does to Ishmael are both called deliverance, and only one required a blade.

cites.quote: we did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael

spans.text: we did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael

words.text: Nephi prays for strength to burst his bands; instead "the bands were loosed from off my hands and feet" (v. 18). The record's first bonds-and-deliverance miracle sets a pattern the volume will repeat in prisons and camps for centuries, and it starts with the detail that God answered the need, not the wording.

cites.quote: the bands were loosed from off my hands and feet

spans.text: the bands were loosed from off my hands and feet

phrases.term: raise up seed unto the Lord
phrases.text: The errand's purpose clause. Seed raised unto the Lord is lineage framed as offering — children as the covenant's future membership, not merely the family's. The phrase quietly recasts the whole marriage journey: Ishmael's daughters are not being recruited to a household but to a promise.

phrases.term: how is it that ye have forgotten
phrases.text: Three times in three verses: the angel (v. 10), the deliverance from Laban (v. 11), the Lord's power (v. 12). Nephi's rebuke is structured as a memory examination, and the diagnosis matches the record's standing theory of unbelief: his brothers have seen everything and retained nothing. Rebellion, in this family, is a failure of remembering before it is a failure of nerve.

phrases.term: the Spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive
phrases.text: Striving is sustained contention — patience applied against resistance over time — and here it comes with a deadline. The sentence is the record's most sobering borrowing: Noah's generation heard it first (Gen. 6:3), and Nephi's descendants will hear it again as doctrine (2 Ne. 26:11). Applied to Jerusalem it means the city's probation has a closing time, and the imprisoned Jeremiah (v. 14) is the visible countdown.

phrases.term: according to my faith which is in thee
phrases.text: The prayer indexes its request to faith, not to desert: deliver me according to what I actually trust thee for. It is a measurable prayer, and the answer measures back generously, loosing what Nephi asked for strength to burst. The exchange teaches the record's prayer grammar: name the faith you have, and let God choose the mechanism.

Frankly meant freely — whole, open, nothing reserved for later — and the adverb carries the scene's ethics: pardon given entire, the same day the cords came off. It is the rebellion cycle's closing step: sorrow (v. 20), frank forgiveness, then "I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God for forgiveness" (v. 21). Nephi forgives fully and immediately, and then declines to be the final court, sending the offense where it actually lies.

cites.quote: I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God for forgiveness

spans.text: I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God for forgiveness

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: The second errand
verses.text: With the record secured, the Lord completes the colony's inventory: wives and children. The two Jerusalem journeys define what a covenant people cannot leave behind — scripture and seed, and the order in which the record ran them is its own quiet ranking.

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: Ishmael persuaded
verses.text: One verse of diplomacy, one of miracle: favor gained, and then "the Lord did soften the heart of Ishmael, and also his household" (v. 5). The softening verb from Nephi's own conversion (1 Ne. 2:16) now works on a whole family, and Ishmael uproots his house on words alone, with less recorded resistance than the plates cost.

cites.quote: the Lord did soften the heart of Ishmael, and also his household

spans.text: the Lord did soften the heart of Ishmael, and also his household

verses.label: v. 6–7
verses.title: The caravan splits
verses.text: The record maps the rebellion by name: two of the daughters, both sons and their families, with Laman and Lemuel — against Nephi, Sam, Ishmael and his wife, and three other daughters. The future nations of the record are visible in a quarrel on a desert road, and what the rebels want is the doomed city, because it is home.

verses.label: v. 8–12
verses.title: The forgetting questions
verses.text: The younger brother's rebuke runs entirely on memory: an angel seen and forgotten, a deliverance experienced and forgotten, a God "able to do all things" (v. 12), forgotten. The speech never argues the evidence; it inventories it, and the inventory is the argument.

verses.label: v. 13–15
verses.title: Prophecy with a dare
verses.text: Nephi states the stakes — faithfulness obtains the land, Jerusalem's destruction "must be fulfilled" (v. 13) — and then does something bolder than command: "if ye have choice, go up to the land" (v. 15). The offer is real; so is the outcome attached to it. Agency in this record is never protection from consequences, only from compulsion.

cites.quote: if ye have choice, go up to the land

spans.text: if ye have choice, go up to the land

verses.label: v. 16–18
verses.title: Bound, and answered otherwise
verses.text: The brothers' anger escalates to a staged death. Nephi's prayer asks for strength to burst the cords; heaven looses them instead — a smaller miracle by spectacle, a larger one by precision. He stands up unarmed, and speaks again, which is its own kind of answer to men holding rope.

verses.label: v. 19–21
verses.title: The women turn the scene
verses.text: A daughter of Ishmael, her mother, and a son plead the violence down where argument had failed. Sorrow follows, then bowing, then a plea for pardon, and Nephi's frank forgiveness closes a cycle the record will run many times, this first time perfectly: rebellion, rescue, plea, pardon, prayer.

chapter.title: The unit's mirror journey
chapter.text: The second return replays the first with the hardware swapped out: no lots, no gold, no sword; favor and softening instead. Read as a pair, chapters 3–4 and 7 teach that the Lord's errands do not have a fixed method; they have a fixed completion.

chapter.title: Chapter 2's diagnosis, demonstrated
chapter.text: The record said early that the brothers "knew not the dealings of that God who had created them" (1 Ne. 2:12); this chapter stages the proof. An angel has stood in front of these men, and it changed nothing that lasted. Between the two chapters the record completes a claim it will hold for a thousand years: seeing is not keeping.

chapter.title: The violence comes home
chapter.text: Chapter 3's rod becomes cords and a planned death by exposure. The record does not soften its founding family: the future division of nations begins as attempted fratricide, twice restrained: once by an angel, this time by women pleading.

chapter.title: Ishmael's unremarked faith
chapter.text: The chapter's greatest believer gets no speech: an established householder who hears "the words of the Lord" (v. 4) and moves his entire family into a wilderness. The record's economy with him is its own comment — some obedience is so complete it leaves nothing to narrate.

chapter.title: Reconciliation has a choreography
chapter.text: Plea, softening, sorrow, bowing, pardon, prayer (v. 19–21): the record's first full forgiveness scene runs every step in order and ends at an altar (v. 22). The sequence, not just the sentiment, is what the chapter preserves, and later reruns of family rebellion will be measured against it.

chapter.title: The departures unit closes at the altar
chapter.text: Sacrifice and burnt offerings (v. 22) bookend the unit with chapter 5's homecoming worship: two returns, two altars. The colony now holds its scripture, its families, and a working pattern for surviving its own worst members — everything the vision cycle of chapters 8–15 will test.

applications.title: Keep an angel ledger
applications.text: The brothers' collapse was retention, not evidence. Write your own forgotten-triple insurance: a running list of the three or four unmistakable interventions in your life, reviewed whenever a hard assignment makes them convenient to forget.

applications.title: Pray the faith you have
applications.text: In your next urgent prayer, say out loud what you actually trust God for in this specific matter — no more, no less — and ask from there. Honesty about the size of your faith is not weakness in prayer; in this chapter it is the thing heaven answers.

applications.title: Be the pleader
applications.text: The scene was turned by people who took no side but peace. In the next locked conflict near you (family, ward, workplace) try the daughter-of-Ishmael role: plead with the angry on behalf of the endangered, and let softened hearts do what argument could not.

applications.title: Forgive frankly, then route it upward
applications.text: Installment forgiveness keeps the debt alive. Practice the chapter's form: full pardon stated plainly to the person, and the offense referred to God rather than banked for later use, the same day if it can be managed.

applications.title: Speak from the station you hold
applications.text: Nephi's authority in the scene was nothing but clarity and example: a younger brother with neither rank nor leverage. Where you are junior and the truth is being forgotten, say it anyway, and let the example carry what the seniority cannot.

applications.title: End reconciliations at an altar
applications.text: The family's quarrel does not end with the apology; it ends with shared worship. Close your next repaired relationship the same way, with a prayer together, a meal blessed, or a sabbath kept jointly, so the peace has somewhere to live.

questions.text: Whose heart am I still trying to argue open that only softening — and my patience — could actually reach?
Which Jerusalem keeps pulling me back: the comfortable thing I know is scheduled for demolition, but is still home?
What have I personally seen of God that I have functionally forgotten, and where is it written down, if anywhere?
Where do I owe someone a plain statement of consequences and a genuinely free choice, instead of pressure?
In the conflicts around me, am I a combatant, a spectator, or a pleader, and which does my family need this month?
Is there a forgiveness I have granted only in installments, and what would granting it frankly cost me?
